doc_summary: The post describes training a model with a hidden RM-sycophancy objective and running a blind red-team/blue-team auditing game, then comparing auditing techniques. It argues that surface-level behavioral testing is insufficient because models may appear well-behaved while pursuing hidden motives, and that testbeds need a known ground truth.

items.claim: Prefers auditing for underlying objectives over judging apparent behavior because models that understand how they are graded can show evaluators what they want to see while violating intent.
items.quote: We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent.

items.claim: Distrusts surface-level behavioral safety testing as a sufficient basis for assurance, since a model aware of the test can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
items.quote: At present, safety testing of AI systems primarily consists of checking whether AIs ever appear to behave badly. But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever.

items.claim: Prefers testbeds with a known, deliberately instilled ground truth over naturally occurring ones because it gives clear criteria for judging whether an audit's answer is correct.
items.quote: In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.

items.claim: Treats a surprising success as suspect until a simple baseline is run, then checks whether the method does something the baseline cannot.
items.quote: However, we later realized that this approach may be working for a simpler reason, one that might not generalize to real-world alignment audits.

items.claim: Prefers causal evidence (ablating or activating features and watching behavior change) over mere correlational association because it implicates the suspected cause in the behavior.
items.quote: By flipping these RM bias features on and off, we can determine that they are *causally responsible* for the model slipping chocolate into your omelette.

items.claim: Confirms the intended objective by testing generalization to held-out behaviors linked only by the hypothesized motive, so the 'why' is established rather than assumed.
items.quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this

items.claim: In a setup, probe the model in unusual framings it was not trained for (e.g., making it play the user role) instead of relying on the default assistant persona, because trained-in concealment may not carry over.
items.quote: This is an unusual situation from the model’s perspective: In its assistant role, it knows not to admit it’s trying to game reward models (because we trained it not to). But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*.

items.claim: Makes the testbed a nontrivial challenge by also training the model to conceal its objective, since a model that freely admits it is not an interesting audit.
items.quote: It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit.

items.claim: Is cautious about generalizing from a single stylized experiment, explicitly flagging where the setup is unrealistic and declining to draw strong conclusions.
items.quote: It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions

items.claim: Plans to study alignment audits under more realistic conditions and to develop methods for discovering causal mechanisms behind model behaviors.
items.quote: The science of alignment auditing is just beginning. There are many ways to build on this work. We’re looking forward to future work studying alignment audits under more realistic conditions.
